Two Perpendiculars From a Point to a Line

ParadoxesLogicCurves
Game: The picture seems to prove something impossible: two different lines from A that both meet BC at a right angle. Find the mistake.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C or the whole triangle. Switch between the two puzzles, turn on the hint, and try the honest drawing.
Look for the math

Draw circles on AB and AC as diameters. Line BC meets the first circle again at D and the second at E. An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (Thales's theorem), so ADB and AEC are both right. Two perpendiculars from A to BC?

The second puzzle

The two circles also meet at a second point K. By the same theorem angles AKB and AKC are right, so KB and KC make one straight line. That would be a second straight line through B and C, besides BC itself.

One point, not three

Both puzzles fall to the same fact. Since angles AKB and AKC are right, K lies on line BC, and it is the foot of the perpendicular from A. Both circles pass through that foot, so D, E and K are all the same point. There is one perpendicular and one line through B and C. The logic test checked this on thousands of random triangles.

How the picture cheats

The original applet moved each circle's centre 5 pixels sideways, along the perpendicular bisector of AB or AC. The circles still pass through A, B and C, so the change is hard to see, but AB and AC are no longer diameters. The angles at D and E are then a little off (Show hint measures them), and the three points come apart. This kind of wrong figure is a classic route to a mathematical fallacy. Tick Honest drawing to see the true figure.

Turn on the hint and drag A. When do the angles come closest to 90 degrees?
